text: Seven more, a sentence or two each. Locks, mutexes and semaphores. A mutex allows exactly one holder. A semaphore allows up to some number, say five downloads at once. And a reentrant lock can be taken again by the thread that already holds it, so recursive code doesn't deadlock on itself. An atomic operation completes in one indivisible step: no other thread can see it half done. Adding one to the counter isn't atomic. Compare-and-swap instructions make it so, or a lock held around the whole thing. Thread-safe code behaves correctly when many threads call it at once. Avoid shared mutable state, guard it with a lock, or best, keep it in one thread and send that thread work through a thread-safe queue. Share by communicating, not by sharing memory. In a livelock, threads keep running but make no progress: they react to each other and retry, like two people stepping aside the same way, again and again. The CPU looks busy, so it's harder to spot than a deadlock. Randomized backoff usually breaks it. Starvation is a thread that never gets the resource, because others keep getting priority, like a low-priority thread that never wins a lock. Fair locks help, and so does not handing out shared resources by priority. A thread pool keeps a fixed set of reusable workers and a queue of tasks. You skip creating a thread per task, and you bound how many run at once. Map a function over a list with it, and the results come back in input order. And a future is a claim ticket for a result that isn't ready yet. Start the work, take the ticket at once, and collect the value later, by blocking on it or awaiting it. All of this was about code running at the same time. Just as hard is code that has to keep changing without breaking. Next: designing objects.
